rationale: habanero extract and acute swallowing timing — Thirteen participants completed the Parkinson crossover. Four videofluoroscopy timing measures showed no clear difference after extract versus placebo. Ground cayenne and symptom severity were outside the comparison.

placebo-controlled oral capsaicin film in mixed chronic dysphagia — In 42 gastrostomy-fed patients including people with Parkinson, oral capsaicin film reduced pooled immediate swallowing reflex latency. Sustained latency change was inconclusive. The abstract supplies no Parkinson subgroup estimate or ground cayenne exposure.
aerosolized extract in an uncontrolled dysphagia series — The 16-patient series reports clinical use and associations without a Parkinson subgroup response or controlled severity estimate.
capsaicin drink or chilled capsaicin probe and water swallow signs — The abstract reports pooled signs without a Parkinson subgroup or separate probe temperature effect.

aerosolized capsaicin and endoscopic swallowing in mixed neurogenic dysphagia — Interim diagnosis footnotes conflict. Final pooled counts establish a cough response in all four Parkinson-labeled aerosol participants and bound swallowing responses at two to four of four versus zero to one of five. Exact swallowing counts and severity remain unavailable.

capsaicin jelly and green tea swallows in a mixed cohort — Nine participants included five with Parkinson. Pooled swallow latency and duration fell five minutes after jelly. No Parkinson subgroup data or ground cayenne. Same authors report follow-up in 2002, with participant overlap unknown.

capsaicin jelly and instrumental timing in Parkinson — Fifteen with Parkinson and no overt aspiration took contrast jelly with and without capsaicin. Mean pharyngeal delay and passage times were shorter with capsaicin, with no significance tests given. The preparation and short-term endpoint differ from the claim.

related ground red chili and non-Parkinson gargle — A filtered ground red chili gargle increased mean saliva-swallow counts from baseline at 20 minutes in ten healthy adults. Cultivar, between-condition effect and clinical Parkinson outcomes were unverified.

related ground red chili and non-Parkinson physiology — Twelve healthy adults chewed fewer times and had altered manometry with commercial ground red chili in mochi. Cayenne cultivar and Parkinson dysphagia severity were untested.

capsaicin and swallowing-related breathing with cohort and results unavailable — Miura and colleagues presented a study on capsaicin, swallowing apnea duration, and breathing pattern. The title provides no preparation, population or result. No publicly readable counterpart was identified. It leaves ground cayenne and Parkinson swallowing severity unresolved.

qualitative dysphagia response during vinegar and levodopa coadministration — The single postoperative case involves a different coadministered ingredient and gives no swallowing severity score. It did not examine cayenne.

oral capsaicin jelly and six-month dysphagia follow-up — The 15 participants had Parkinson or cerebrovascular disease; 12 completed. Four reported improvement, three had reduced laryngeal penetration, group videofluoroscopy change was inconclusive, and two developed pneumonia. No placebo, Parkinson subgroup result or ground cayenne.

nonpungent CH-19 Sweet capsinoid seasoning on a VF jelly — The 17-person mixed dysphagia report describes changes in instrumental timing and movement. There was no Parkinson subgroup or group clinical swallowing result for ground cayenne. Earlier five-person progress report is the same project.
inhaled diagnostic stimulus — The registered and published analyses characterize cough physiology. No culinary or swallowing treatment contrast.
inhaled diagnostic stimulus — Posted outcomes describe cough sensitivity and separate swallowing testing by disease group. No ground cayenne treatment contrast.

aerosolized capsaicin used to measure reflex cough — The one-arm study used capsaicin during testing before and after cough training. Reflex cough peak flow did not clearly change. It gives no ground cayenne or swallowing difficulty estimate.

acute pharyngeal catheter challenge with CH-19 Sweet capsiate — In 12 older patients with aspiration pneumonia, mean reflex latency was 16.3 s with water and 6.1 s at 100 nM capsiate. Extract, catheter route and cohort differ from the frozen claim, and no Parkinson subgroup was reported.

red-pepper-seasoned cabbage and swallowing reflex latency — Within-group latency shortened in older adults without dysphagia. The study had no unexposed control and removed the red pepper slices and pickling liquid before serving.
topical aural capsaicin and mixed dysphagia — Pooled swallowing outcomes favored the intervention on some measures. Parkinson subgroup contained three participants with no separate effect.

swallowing endoscopy after nebulized capsaicin in a stroke case — After a week, secretion ratings improved and silent aspiration for IDDSI Level 1 liquid remained unchanged. Later measurements followed combined therapy and used different test consistencies. This is an uncontrolled post-stroke inhalation case.
aerosolized cayenne and cough — A mixed cohort included three participants with Parkinson disease. The study measured cough and supplied no Parkinson-specific swallowing estimate.
capsaicin wafer and swallow timing — No clear swallowing timing improvement in the small wafer comparison.

capsaicin as part of a Parkinson cough training program — The intervention combines cough practice, feedback and aerosol stimulus. It gives no isolated capsaicin or swallowing difficulty treatment estimate.
capsaicin solution and mixed dysphagia population — The active arm showed a within-arm change. The abstract does not give a between-group or Parkinson-specific estimate.
oral liquid extract and cough provocation in healthy adults — Transient cough suppression occurred in 23 of 25. The project gives no Parkinson swallowing difficulty measure.

The original 2018 and 2019 reports and 2020 abstract share the research line. Acute capsaicin elicited reflex swallowing, while later air-evoked swallows decreased after prolonged direct laryngeal contact. The 85 refers to the later article total. Oral culinary exposure and clinical Parkinson severity were not studied.

The independent S270 poster reports swallows evoked by isolated capsaicin in mineral oil compared with mineral oil alone. Anesthetized non-Parkinson rats were assessed on reflex initiation. The poster supplies no analyzed denominator and no clinical difficulty outcome.

In separate healthy-volunteer experiments, short preconditioning with a cayenne-distinct red pepper sauce suspension favored cued swallow precision and continuous exposure did not show the same improvement. The experiments used multiple outcome denominators and assessed physiology rather than symptoms.

The 21-person healthy crossover tests active versus sham cortical stimulation. Both periods receive the same oral capsaicinoids. The volume-per-swallow difference supplies no independent capsaicinoid estimate or Parkinson dysphagia result.
